https://www.dw.com/en/masha-and-the-bear.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JEAw Some signs of the show's popularity in Ukraine could even be seen in the ruins of homes damaged by the 2022 Russian invasion [FILE: March 2022] Image: Rodrigo Abd/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Ukrainian Culture Minister Tetyana Berezhna on Friday said Kyiv had imposed sanctions on the "producers and distributors" of the Russian children's cartoon series "Masha and the Bear," or "Masha i Medved" in the original language. The step will enable Kyiv to seek to remove and demonentize the series on websites like YouTube or streaming services like Netflix in the country. The cartoon about a mischievous young girl's unlikely friendship and adventures with a retired circus bear, loosely based on a Russian oral fairytale of the same name, launched in 2009 and quickly became one of Russia 's most successful televisual exports. Masha and the Bear or Masha i Medved's YouTube channel is among the 50 most-watched in the world, with more than 54 billion views worldwide as of June 2026 Image: Ivan Sekretarev/AP Photo/picture alliance What did the government in Kyiv say about the sanctions? "Ukraine has imposed sanctions against the producers and distributors of the Russian animated series Masha and the Bear," Berezhna said on social media. "This creates legal grounds to block the content in Ukraine and engage international platforms to restrict its monetization and distribution." The show has also faced criticism from allies of Ukraine like Estonia and the UK for allegedly painting Russia in a positive light or for military or Soviet symbols sometimes appearing in the show. "Russian propaganda has no place on children's screens — in Ukraine or anywhere in the world," Berezhna said. In further comments on Facebook, Berezhna said the Ukrainian language channel for the show had 800 million views in 2025 alone. The Ukrainian language channel currently has roughly 18 million subscribers. Worldwide, as of June 2026, the show had more than 54 billion combined views on YouTube, making it one of the 50 most popular feeds on the entire site. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree imposing sanctions on the creators of the show for spreading "pro-Russia narratives" and for posing a threat to Ukrainian national security. They target the studio, the show's founder, and the series' scriptwriter and director. Ukraine said it would seek to have its sanctions mirrored by international partners, potentially widening the restrictions. The story revolves around a curious and sometimes mischievous girl's unlikely friendship with a protective former circus bear Image: Ivan Sekretarev/AP Photo/picture alliance How did the show's makers and the Russian government respond? The company behind the show, Animaccord Animation Studios, has called past allegations that the show contains Russian propaganda "false and defamatory," saying that it operates independently and receives no funding from the government in Moscow. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked about the sanctions on Friday and said that the cartoon series had "conquered the world" by promoting "the finest human qualities." "The fact that Ukraine has launched a war against cartoons, too, likely serves as yet another illustration of the ugly nature" of the authorities in Kyiv, he said. The show has a following across much of Europe — in this case as demonstrated in hay-bale form in Croatia — and even further afield Image: Davor Javorovic/PIXSELL/picture alliance Is 'Masha and the Bear' controversial, and why? The show has been on the radar of Ukrainian authorities for almost a decade. The first complaint by the State Film Agency dates back to 2017, amid the illegal annexation of Crimea and the lower-level war in Ukraine waged by separatists supported by Russia. Since the 2022 full-scale invasion the issue has come into sharper focus still. In June, Kyiv protested against streaming giant Netflix's move to acquire the rights to stream new seasons of "Masha and the Bear." A group of more than 50 British parliamentarians this year appealed to Culture Minister Lisa Nandy to urge streaming platforms to remove the cartoon. They argued that some episodes exposed children to Russian and Soviet military imagery. Several Estonian politicians have also argued that "Masha and the Bear" is an instrument of Russian soft power, not least because of the several amiable bears in its cast. Some Western analysts have warned against exaggerating these fears, though — for instance UK academic Mark Galeotti, who wrote an article objecting to the British lawmakers' appeal in July, saying the show was not "the most elevated of television," but "it is cute and it has a big heart." In its earlier days, "Masha i Medved" was also a topic of some controversy in Russia. It sometimes drew critical comparisons to Western children's shows and prompted debate on whether it was contradicting traditional values about the roles of girls and fathers in Russian society, given Masha's mischievous nature and her paternal bear's gentle use of positive reinforcement rather than correctional discipline. https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/05/mag.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter belengette az autópálya-koncesszió felülvizsgálatát Gazdaság Vida Benjámin Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Ahogy vállaltuk, felszámoljuk a közpénzzabrálást a dohány- és a kaszinókoncesszióknál. Felkészül a 35 éves autópálya-koncesszió” – írta Magyar Péter miniszterelnök szombaton a Facebook-oldalán . Vitézy Dávid közlekedési és beruházási miniszter azt már június közepén bejelentette, hogy felülvizsgálják a dohány- és kaszinókoncessziókat, valamint az ezekhez kötődő szabályozásokat. A koncessziók felülvizsgálatát és kezelését a Közlekedési és Beruházási Minisztérium látja el, így az autópálya- és a reptéri vasút koncessziója mellett a trafikok és a kaszinók ügye is Vitézy Dávidékhoz került . A legutóbbi kormányzati sajtótájékoztatón pedig az is kiderült , hogy a kormány az Országgyűlés elé terjeszti Szabályozott Tevékenységek Felügyeleti Hatóságának a koncessziós szerződésekkel kapcsolatos hatáskörének megszüntetését. Az előző kormány 2022-ben bocsátotta koncesszióba 35 évre a hazai autópálya- és gyorsforgalmi úthálózat nagy részét. Egy magántőkealapok alkotta konzorcium, a Magyar Koncessziós Infrastruktúra Fejlesztő Zrt. (MKIF) nyerte el a szerződést. A konzorcium tulajdonosi hátteréről csak azután lehetett többet meg tudni, hogy a Szabad Európa kiperelte a szerződés mellékleteit: a magántőkealapok Mészáros Lőrinchez és Szíjj Lászlóhoz tartoznak. Az MKIF-cégek az első években jelentős nyereséget termeltek, és osztalékot fizettek Mészáros Lőrincnek és Szíjj Lászlónak, ami szokatlan a koncessziók kezdeti időszakában. Ami szintén feltűnő, hogy az MKIF által megvalósított új építések és sávbővítések négyszer-ötször drágábbak , mint a közepesen fejlett és fejlődő országok koncessziói esetében. Az Európai Bizottság 2022-ben indított kötelezettségszegési eljárást a koncesszió miatt. A Bizottság úgy indokolta a döntést, hogy a koncesszió nem volt átlátható a becsült szerződéses érték tekintetében, nem hárítja át kellő mértékben a működéssel kapcsolatos kockázatot, és indokolatlanul hosszú időre szól, így sérti az uniós jogot. Ebsen Salling Larsen, a military analyst at the Center for Joint Operations at the Danish Defence Academy, said it is normal for Danish ships, helicopters or planes to go out to monitor Russian state-owned ships and warships. Sometimes this prompts Russian crew to point weapons at them or use a tracking radar. But Monday’s incident, during which Russian flares were fired at a Danish helicopter, was unusual and marked a “change in pattern”. “There’s an ongoing tension and the incident yesterday talks to that increased tension somewhat,” said Salling Larsen. “If you go back to the cold war you have more incidents of ships bumping into each other and so forth. https://www.middleeasteye.net/explainers.text: Sanctions on Israeli settlements: Here’s what Europe is saying and doing Daniel Tester Published date: 9 September 2026 16:11 BST | Last update: 1 week 6 days ago Relations between Israel and European states have deteriorated after the UK led moves on Tuesday to impose sanctions against Israeli settlements . In London, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, using some of the harshest language by a government minister about Israel, said that the decision came amid the “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists”. In Paris, meanwhile, his opposite number Jean-Noel Barrot announced similar measures, saying that “France cannot, through its trade, support a situation that threatens the security of Israelis and Palestinians alike”. In a joint statement , they, along with the foreign ministers of Spain, Ireland Norway and others, confirmed their intention to “introduce national and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with settlements which are illegal under international law, or that they are actively considering these and other measures, in accordance with their national procedures”. Several countries, notably Sweden, Denmark and Finland, later stated that they would only impose sanctions as part of joint EU action rather than unilaterally, according to Israeli media reports . New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters The announcements came amid growing international condemnation of attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, as well as the expansion of settlements by the government of Benjamin Netanyahu. Several European countries previously issued sanctions following a 2024 ruling from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that the settlements were illegal under international law. The moves come amid deadlock in the EU over proposals to introduce an EU-wide ban on settlement goods, with key states such as Germany and Italy stalling. UK The UK played a leading role in Tuesday’s 12-nation sanctions on settlements, with the joint statement released at the same time as a speech from Miliband in the UK parliament. The UK will now have some of the strongest policies against the settlements, targeting the import of goods from settlements, investment in settlement businesses and properties, and advertisement of services in settlements. Announcing the measures, Miliband accused the Israeli government of turning a “blind eye” to the displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank, where over 450,000 Israeli settlers now live, adding : “The action we are taking today is against the government of Israel, not its people." UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announces UK sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on 8 September 2026 (House of Parliament/AFP) Israel lashed out in response, closing the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, ejecting British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center, and banning 11 British MPs from entering Israel (none have government roles). Relations between London and Tel Aviv have worsened in recent months, with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu sparking fury in Westminster in August by referring to the UK as the “Islamic Republic of Britain”. France Until this week, France had not banned imports of goods from Israeli settlements, despite efforts from opposition lawmakers and ex-diplomats . But in a statement on X on Tuesday, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said that “France cannot, through its trade, support a situation that threatens the security of Israelis and Palestinians alike”. Paris previously sanctioned around 50 individual settlers, plus some of the organisations that run outposts that have not been approved by the Israeli government. France has also led calls for a ban on trade with the settlements at an EU level, where talks have stalled for months. “The settlements are illegal,” Barrot previously said on 5 September, citing the ICJ ruling. “It is not normal that the European Union can support this trade.” He added that the EU’s response should match the swift action it took to halt imports from Crimea following its occupation by Russia in 2014. “This is the same thing that we must do with the illegal settlements.” Spain One of Europe’s firmest critics of Israel, the government headed by centre-left Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez banned imports from Israeli settlements in September 2025. Under the law, all produce from anywhere in Israel or the occupied territories must specify its postcode of origin, with penalties for non-compliance. Also banned are advertisements for services based in West Bank settlements. In line with the law, Spain said in December that it had ordered seven companies, which it did not name, to remove listings for rental properties in settlements. It later investigated when Israeli firms advertised settlement properties at an international tourism fair in Madrid in January. Demonstrators hold a canvas with a detail from Pablo Picasso's Guernica next to a giant Palestinian flag in San Sebastian, Spain, in January 2024 (AFP) Spain has issued other measures to curb its involvement in Israel’s genocide in Gaza and the war on Iran : in October 2025, for example, it issued an embargo on the sale of weapons and dual-use goods to Israel, and a ban on imports of Israeli-made military goods to Spain, albeit with some exceptions . Madrid has also prohibited vessels transporting fuel for the Israeli military from using its ports, and planes supplying Israel with military equipment from crossing its airspace. The measures have damaged Spanish relations with Israel, which in 2024 recalled its ambassador after Spain recognised Palestinian statehood. Madrid in turn pulled its ambassador from Tel Aviv the following year. Relations with the US have also suffered, with President Donald Trump hitting Spain with fresh tariffs in June, and threatening to cut off US trade completely in July. Ireland Although a signatory to Tuesday’s joint statement, Ireland had previously banned the import of goods from settlements in July, amid wide support for Palestine and criticism of Israel across the country. A law banning goods and services from Israeli settlements was initially proposed in 2018, but shelved amid fears it could fall foul of EU trade regulations. Provisions within the bill to ban services based in illegal settlements were dropped after they were rejected by senators from Ireland’s centre-right governing coalition, fearful it might cause economic harm and a backlash from the US . The change prompted anger from opposition lawmakers, who said that the legislation had been “watered down”, and was not compliant with international law. Under the current law, websites such as Airbnb, which has its European headquarters in Dublin, face no restrictions on advertising property rentals in the illegal settlements to Irish customers. But the ban on goods was nonetheless criticised by Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel. “Did the Irish fall into a vat of Guinness?” he posted on X, calling the new law an act of “diplomatic intoxication”. Netherlands The Netherlands banned the import of goods produced in Israeli settlements in May, with the law due to come into effect on 22 September. But the measures, which will apply for a fixed three-year period, do not prohibit trade in services based in settlements, other than financial services directly relating to the import of banned goods. Relations between Amsterdam and Tel Aviv have worsened since the law was announced. Israel expelled two Dutch representatives from the US-led International Gaza Support Center in the Israeli city of Kiryat Gat on 25 August. Norway In June, Norway’s government proposed a law banning the import and export of all goods to and from Israeli settlements. Public consultation on the bill ends on 19 September. The proposal also includes a trade ban on “services related to the construction, renovation, purchase or sale of property” in the settlements, and “acquiring businesses with headquarters and production”. Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, right, and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas in Oslo, Norway in February 2026 (AFP) Announcing the proposals in June, Espen Barth Eide, Norway’s foreign minister, said: “The settlements undermine the basis for a Palestinian state. “Norwegian citizens and Norwegian companies must not contribute to maintaining this development. With this legislative proposal, the government takes a clear stance”. Belgium In July, Belgium’s cabinet announced that it had approved a ban on imports of settlement goods, just before parliament closed for its summer recess until October. Full details of the law, which awaits review before it takes effect, have not been made public. Belgium stopped offering consular services to its citizens living in Israeli settlements in January. Sweden Stockholm’s decision to align itself with the UK, France and others on Tuesday appears to be a hardening of its position. Back in April, it only proposed creating tariffs on settlement goods imported at the EU level. That measure, intended to “differentiate this trade from other trade”, according to Sweden’s foreign ministry in April, fell short of calling for a trade ban. But Sweden’s foreign minister, Maria Stenergard, said on Tuesday that her government now “believes that more needs to be done to reduce trade with Israeli settlements”, which she said “violate international law and undermine the two-state solution”. Denmark Denmark was also a signatory to the 12-country statement announcing a prospective ban. “Israel's settlement policy is illegal & undermines a two-state solution. E1 plans are unacceptable,” Foreign Minister Lars Loekke Rasmussen said on Tuesday. Demonstrators protest as part of “All of Denmark on the Streets for a Free Palestine” at Christiansborg Palace Square, Copenhagen in August 2025 (AFP) But Denmark caused confusion when it told Haaretz on Wednesday that it would either impose national restrictions or instead support EU measures to bring in such restrictions. The latter move would amount to little change on its previous position, as the embassy said that Denmark had “for some time” called for an EU-wide trade ban on settlements. Finland Finland also signed the 12-country statement pledging to ban settlement goods on Tuesday, although it has not yet provided further details on its proposed policy. A statement posted by Finland’s foreign ministry on Tuesday said that the “viability of the two-state solution is being steadily undermined by settlement expansion and escalating settler violence. This must stop. International law must be upheld and [the] path to peace preserved,” the ministry added. Finland has generally maintained a cautious foreign policy since it became a Nato member in 2023, not least because it depends on US security assurances against its neighbour, Russia. But the move to ban settlement goods comes as support for the US and Israel has fallen amid the US-Israeli war on Iran. Iceland Iceland was also among the 12 countries announcing a ban on settlements on Tuesday, although it has yet to formally comment. The announcement came hours after Trump posted a map on Truth Social that appeared to show Iceland as part of the US, prompting Iceland to summon the American ambassador. Iceland joined South Africa’s long-stalled genocide case against Israel at the ICJ in March. Poland While Warsaw has been opposed to full sanctions against Israel, it has voiced increasing disquiet in recent years about proposals for illegal settlements. In August, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that the plans to build in the West Bank’s E1 area were a “flagrant breach of international law”. In a signal that it was mulling sanctions against settlements, it said: “We are communicating with the EU’s diplomacy and our European partners to come up with a joint response to these measures.” Portugal Portugal added its name to the list of countries banning settlement goods on Tuesday amid growing domestic discontent over Israeli conduct in the West Bank and Gaza. A statement posted by the country’s foreign ministry said that Portugal “has consistently defended and advocated” for banning settlement goods in private EU discussions. Former Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Costa currently leads the European Council. The EU This week’s announcements on sanctions on Israeli settlements came amid long-standing deadlock on the issue at the EU. France and Sweden previously proposed measures against settlement imports at the EU level, only for it to stall amid opposition from Germany and Italy , two of the continent’s largest economies. Germany has for decades been among Tel Aviv’s firmest allies in Europe, and currently faces a case at the ICJ over its weapons sales to Israel during its genocide in Gaza. Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of fuelling diplomatic isolation after UK sanctions Read More » Italy, meanwhile, has seen its ties with Israel flourish under right-wing Prime Minister Georgia Meloni, although they have lost momentum in recent months amid Rome’s tepid support for the US-Israeli war on Iran. Both countries were also notable for their absence in Tuesday’s joint declaration - but Johann Wadephul, Germany’s foreign minister from the embattled Christian Democratic Union party, still insists that Berlin is opposed to Israeli settlements in the West Bank. “We have a clear position on settlement policy: it is inconsistent with international law,” he said in August, adding that he had “made this clear” to the Israeli government that month. Other countries that have opposed EU action on settlements include Austria , where a right-wing government is in charge, and Slovenia , the first country in Europe to ban imports of goods from Israeli settlements in August 2025. But new conservative Prime Minister Janez Jansa overturned that decision during his first week in office in June and also lifted other measures against Israel, including an arms embargo and entry ban on Netanyahu and other officials. The moves were welcomed by Israel, where Foreign Minister Gideon Saar called Jansa a “bold leader and true friend”, and announced that Israel would open an embassy in Ljubljana (it had previously run consular services from neighbouring Austria). Make us a preferred source on Google Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save A downtown Galt bookstore has found itself at the centre of a social media wave, with its new owners saying a steady stream of online videos has brought new customers through the doors and created a community far beyond Cambridge. Woolf & Company, at 25 Main St., unit 101, was previously Rookery Books before Shelby Shapiro and her husband, David Brisky, took over the store last September. The couple had talked about one day owning a bookstore, but the opportunity came sooner than expected when a former colleague connected them with the previous owner. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW “We weren’t looking for bookstores for sale. It was just we were in the middle of our life and an opportunity arose and we said, ‘Wow, this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity, let’s take it,’” Shapiro said. Shapiro had already spent years working in bookstores, including Book City in Toronto, Words Worth Books in Waterloo and A Second Look Books in downtown Kitchener. She said the work gave her a collection of specialized skills and stories that eventually became part of conversations with Brisky. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW The couple did not make major changes to the way the store was run when they took over. Instead, they brought different skills to what was already there. “The previous owner set these great foundations and we just kind of added fuel to the fire because we have more resources and we feel very lucky in that way,” said Brisky, who had experience with filming and social media. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW The couple began posting consistently on social media around February and, by June, they noticed the attention starting to grow significantly. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Brisky said the store’s social media reach expanded as platforms began connecting its videos with audiences interested in the content. The effect was soon noticeable in the store, Shapiro noted. She said customers began arriving already knowing her name or asking for books they had seen her discuss online. Some of the more obscure books she talked about, which previously attracted little interest, started selling out at the store and elsewhere. The couple also began hearing from people around the world who had found the bookstore through social media. Shapiro said people have sent them photos of themselves buying books she had recommended in places including Poland and Lithuania. She said the appeal goes beyond simply selling books, adding people are looking for places where they can connect with others without everything being transactional, particularly after the isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW “To me, it’s about having a space and offering a personal relationship with people,” she said. The bookstore’s videos also give people a way to experience the store virtually, she said. People watching the videos can see the owners and employees joking around, recommending books and working together, creating what Shapiro described as an “immersive experience.” Brisky said someone contacted the bookstore several months ago and offered money toward a book giveaway. The couple filmed the giveaway and posted it online, where the video received millions of views. Since then, people have continued donating money to a fund, allowing the bookstore to give away thousands of dollars worth of books. “That was a genuine surprise,” he said. “That just came out of nowhere and it spawned this very wholesome experience that we get to deliver.” The sudden attention has also brought changes behind the scenes. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW The owners said the store was already busy before the social media growth, but last month was “busier than Christmas had been last year.” That has meant more books to process, more shipments, more boxes and more work outside of helping customers on the sales floor, Brisky said. The couple had already hired an employee, Hayden Lyle, before the social media attention took off. They later hired a video editor, who now remotely handles the large amount of footage generated by the store. Shapiro said the biggest change has been getting used to working in a store where a camera is filming throughout the day, adding being filmed all day requires employees to be aware that ordinary conversations or moments at work could eventually be seen by tens of thousands of people. “It’s a different style of working for sure,” she said. Despite the growth, the couple said they are not assuming the current level of attention will last forever. “We’re so grateful for what we’re experiencing now, but we’re not expecting or anticipating everyone to support us to this capacity forever,” Brisky said. “We’re trying to figure out how to make it a sustainable thing for everyone.” ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW The couple’s long-term goal is to use the bookstore as more than a retail space, including potentially hosting community events, providing space for organizations and raising money for causes. https://europeanforum.net/elections-on-t.text: Elections on the frontline of hybrid war: lessons from Latvia’s battle against Russian digital warfare Published on October 12, 2026 On October 3 rd , Latvians cast their vote in the 15 th Saeima elections, the national parliament of the Baltic state. Former prime minister Evika Siliņa resigned in May earlier this year following the political crisis caused by Ukrainian drones striking Latvian soil, diverted by Russian electronics. Latvia remained stable in the period coming up to the elections however, defying expectations of unrest and (successful) Russian interference after the fall of the government. This was not the first Russian destabilizing attempt that Latvia has faced, and they came prepared. How does Russian disinformation in Latvia look like and what can other EU member states learn from Latvia’s digital battle? Historic elections First, the election results. Current prime minister Andris (United List) has won the elections in a landslide victory, receiving 35% of all votes, a historic high never reached by any party since Latvia’s independence. When Silina resigned as PM, Kulbergs (United List) took up the reins. Since then, he has been very active on social media, profiling himself as a regular Latvian, who at the same time can act as a decisive leader. Since Latvia uses a minimum 5% threshold for parties to enter parliament, United List will take up 41 seats in the Saeima, which has a total of one hundred seats. Kulbergs is known for his pro-Ukrainian and pro-EU stance, pitting him against populist parties such as Latvia First and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians, who came in 2 nd and 3 rd place after the United List, with 13% and 11,7% of the votes respectively. Kulberg’s huge victory wasn’t the only historic aspect of the elections however, as voting turnout was the lowest ever in the history of Latvia’s democracy. Only 51,79% of eligible voters participated in the elections, with 806.641 citizens actually casting their vote . This follows a trend set since the first elections in 1993 after the independence, where 89,9% voted. Security, economy and ties to Russia in campaign time The campaign leading up to the elections focused on, unsurprisingly, security and defense issues, indicating the precarious international context Latvia finds itself in. The Baltic states are the eastern-most border of NATO, a position of high geopolitical importance, only elevated by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Security wasn’t the only theme headlining the campaign however, as economic and social issues also found their way into key talking points. Debates on security issues weren’t limited to defense investments or diplomacy talks, as personal ties between party leaders and Russia and Belarus were hot topics. During the campaign, Riga-based online news website ‘ The Insider’ discovered that Jūlija Stepaņenko, leader of the ‘Sovereign Power/Young Latvians’, has dubious family ties . Stepanenko’s father, Sergei Fedotov, owns the majority share of two Russian family businesses, which can directly be linked to military equipment used in the Donbas and Belgorod region. Fedotov reportedly met with Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout, who argued for bureaucratic obstacles to be removed in Russia, which is “sometimes in a hybrid war, sometimes in an open war”. Other parties requested investigations into Stepanenko. Party leader Aleksejs Rosļikovs from For Stability!, who resides in Belarus, also participated in the elections. Rosļikovs fled to Belarus as he was accused of inciting national and ethnic hatred . Now being on Riga’s wanted list, he still lives in Minsk where he frames himself as a martyr, claiming that he and his family are threatened in Latvia. From Belarus, he aims to undermine the Latvian government, comparing for example gas prices between Belarus and Latvia. For Stability did not pass the 5% threshold. ‘People’s Power Force’, a registered political party but not electable during the parliament elections, organized a so-called ‘wise boycott’. They claim that elections with less than 50% turnout are illegitimate and call upon citizens to not use their vote. In their eyes, oligarchs and politicians have stolen the power from the people, and voting would only legitimize the regime. Their mission is to ‘preserve the population in Latvia’ and ‘stop the extinction of the Latvian nation’, demanding the cancellation of state funding for parties and calling for re-elections. According to the website, 43.692 people joined the boycott, of which 12.219 ‘non-citizens’ and 7.262 anonymously joined. Narratives and frames Common frames spread by Russian disinformation networks are focused on the EU or NATO. ‘These frames attempt to undermine the capability or legitimacy of these organizations’, Anete Bērzkalne tells in an interview with PRO International. Bērzkalne works at the Latvian Radio News Service as a disinformation expert and contributes to investigative journalism, specialized in Europe. ‘On the one hand, the EU would be too weak. On the other hand, the EU would be too focused on Brussels, leaving Latvia as a puppet state of the EU.’ NATO is put in a similar light: the transatlantic organization would either not be able to help Latvia or be too aggressive towards Russia. The Baltic states are often accused of the latter as well. Other narratives being spread say that Latvia’s decisions are silly, incompetent or idiotic. Russia also targets specific audiences, namely the ethnic Russians living in Latvia. Russian speakers make up about 25% of the Latvian population , making it the biggest ethnic minority in the country. Russian sources claim that the Russian diaspora is being repressed. Over the last few years, Russian language in Latvian education has been declining, a trend Russia uses to reinforce their story. Similar to rhetoric used to legitimize the illegal invasion in Ukraine, the Kremlin is quick to use the term ‘nazi’s in their narratives about the supposed repression of Russians, Bērzkalne points out. How does Russia spread disinformation? On the 31 st of July, Bērzkalne interviewed Jānis Sārts , the director of the Rīga-based NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence (STRATCOMCOE). He talked on various hybrid attacks that Latvia could face during the elections, including malicious use of AI and drone- and cyber-attacks. His expectations weren’t misplaced, although state security services report that while cyber-attack activity was observed , it did not cause any consequences regarding the elections. That isn’t for a lack of trying, however. For instance, two researchers monitored AI-responses regarding questions about the election , including what party the language models recommend. Depending on whether Latvian or Russian was used for the prompt, the responses and linked sources varied greatly. When asked in Russian, the AI-models (ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude) used compromised or even banned websites as sources, such as ‘Sputnik News’. The models also recommended different vote choices, favoring parties like ‘For Stability!’, ‘Sovereign Power’ and ‘Union of Young Latvians’. The last two, led by aforementioned Stepanenko, were mentioned twice as often compared to when the prompt was asked in Latvian. Latvian television program ‘De Facto’ monitored pro-Kremlin media outlets and found that political candidates supporting Ukraine and sanctions against Russia were often ridiculed. On the other hand, candidates criticizing restrictions on Russian grain transits, for example, were favored. As one in three Latvian internet users make use of AI , manipulation of these models by flooding the network with Kremlin-favored content becomes increasingly interesting for Russia. Social media provide key platforms for disinformation practices, mainly on TikTok and Telegram, Bērzkalne states. ‘Narratives first spread through other digital means can trickle down to social media platforms as well.’. The type of destabilization efforts depends on the platform, for example, Telegram is also used to recruit people for sabotage actions, whereas X shows more bot activity. After the elections, Varis Teivāns, head of the Latvian cyber incident prevention institution , told Latvian Radio that cyber-attackers tried to create websites with similar domain names as popular Latvian news outlets , most likely for malicious purposes. They also tried to find loopholes in the digital environment, not just of election systems, but also the systems of local government and other state institutions. He acknowledged that more attacks were predicted but did not want to speculate on whether the high level of preparedness and investments deterred possible attackers. Fighting back against digital warfare Although it’s hard to say why the intensity of the attacks was less than expected, it’s clear that Latvia is fighting back. In January earlier this year, an inter-institutional group was formed to prevent security threats to the parliamentary elections, consisting of institutions concerned with election processes, state security services and cybersecurity for example. Furthermore, pro-Kremlin parties were monitored preventively , starting in 2025. On recommendation of the VDD (the State Security Service), 400 Russian propaganda websites have been blocked in Latvia since the invasion of Ukraine. In 2022, 80 Russian media outlets were similarly prohibited. Anti-disinformation campaigns were used to educate voters about their role in the elections, how they can recognize disinformation and not spread it themselves. In her work, Anete Bērzkalne also tries to raise awareness about disinformation and how they operate. How malicious narratives and frames aim to create apathy, distrust and dissatisfaction: ‘the main goal is to dissuade people from voting or to encourage them to vote for parties that are more Russia-friendly’, she tells. ‘Everytime when we discover disinformation practices, it’s a judgement call. Do we tell the public and if so, how and when? The goal of the practices is often to spread fear, we don’t want to contribute to that.’ Drawing on an example from TikTok, which said that there would be a Russian election or referendum in January on the annexation of Latvia. ‘It was completely fake, but it looked very scary. So, I published it quite a time later’. When asked about what other EU countries can learn from Latvia’s fight against Russian hybrid warfare, she underlined the importance of understanding how disinformation works and what the intent is behind spreading false narratives. ‘Narratives may seem contradictory but serve the same purpose: creating divisions between Latvians, between EU or NATO member states.’ She finishes: ‘We look at the impact of hybrid attacks, what the goals are. Fear or gathering intelligence, for example?
